 Michael Burgess Senior Sports Journalist · NZ Herald · 20 Nov, 2026 05:00 PM 7 mins to read ‌

 Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Sam Cosgrove wants to move on. 
 The Auckland FC striker has captured headlines across the first few weeks of the A-League season, though not in the way he would have desired. 
 We could have been talking about plenty of things with Cosgrove: backing up his Golden Boot 
 season, adapting to a new coaching staff, taking on a leadership role, or the quest to reach another grand final. Hell, we could even discuss the sandpapergate scandal, given Cosgrove was a decent age-grade cricketer and still follows the sport. 
 But the 29-year-old has been embroiled in off-field drama, after a training ground bust-up with Stuff reporter Andrew Voerman ahead of the opening round. After Cosgrove picked up a two-game ban during the Fifa Intercontinental Cup in August, Auckland FC used a loophole to allow Cosgrove to “serve” his ban via the reserve team. 
 Talking to the media after training last month, Cosgrove faced a series of questions about his non-suspension, before t a heated exchange at the end of the session. It started when Auckland FC chief executive Nick Becker got involved, directly addressing Voerman after the interview had finished but while cameras were still rolling.Cosgrove, ​who was walking away, came back to continue the discussion, swearing at the journalist at one point. 
 Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Twelve days later, Cosgrove received another ban. According to Football Australia, the striker “failed to uphold the expected standards of integrity, dignity and professionalism required of a professional player” and received a two-game ban, though one was suspended, contingent on no further breaches this season. In his first extended interview since then, Cosgrove admitted it was a challenging time. 
 “I found out about the [second] ban when we were over in Brisbane,” Cosgrove tells the Herald . “Obviously it was a decent amount of time after the incident happened, which was disappointing. It messed with the plans for the game a bit. But with football there’s challenges and that was one that I had to deal with ... and the club and Pedro [Moreira] as well, which was unfortunate.” 
 But was it a fair punishment? “Look I’ve still got a one-game suspension hanging over my head, so I don’t want to talk out of line too much,” Cosgrove says. “But obviously we were all a little bit frustrated and disappointed with how the whole thing played out. I’m sure that’s not a surprise to anyone. Hindsight’s a wonderful thing and looking back I should have just walked away from the whole incident before it happened.” 
 Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Cosgrove is also contrite, specifically about the profanities used in the interaction. 
 “I’d like to put on record my apology to anyone that was offended by any of the language that I used,” Cosgrove says. “In my career I’ve done countless media interviews with people back home, [then] obviously in New Zealand and I honestly can’t remember a time when I’ve used inappropriate language on record, which is why I was disappointed that the media outlet in question decided to publicise the interaction after the formal [interview] proceedings had concluded. But I guess that’s the world we live in now. We’ve accepted it, happy to move on.” 
 Auckland FC striker Sam Cosgrove has brought a physical presence to the A-League. Photo / Photosport Moving on is important, after an “up and down” start to this campaign, with five points from four matches. However, Cosgrove was encouraged by the performance in the 0-0 draw against the Wellington Phoenix – especially the second half – as being more of “what we are about”. This early part of this season was always going to be challenging - after all the personnel changes - but Cosgrove is bullish about the future. He is also enjoying more of a leadership role within the squad. 
 “That was [something] I fell into last season,” Cosgrove says. “But sometimes it can quite hard coming in and imposing yourself within a new changing room, just because you don’t want to rub people up the wrong way, if they think you’re coming in too brash.” 
 Playing the villain 
 Cosgrove’s move to New Zealand came at an ideal time. As he told the Herald last October, the former Aberdeen, Birmingham City, Plymouth and Barnsley striker (among many others) had got a bit stale in English football – “lost his spark” - and needed a change. 
 It worked. He made an impression last season, scoring 12 goals and contributing four assists. As well, he quickly became a focal point for opposition fans – with his rugged, physical style of play. He embraces the villain tag – taking it as a compliment. “When you’ve got that target on your back, it’s usually because you are effective,” Cosgrove says. But he is still trying to find the right balance, between the controlled aggression necessary for a target man and giving away cheap fouls or bookings, which can be so costly. 
 “That’s a dilemma that I’ve been trying to work out for the past 12 or 13 years in my career, where that line is and how not to step over that line,” Cosgrove says. “Believe it or not, I’m a hell of a lot better than I used to be 10 years ago. It used to be red cards, now it’s only yellow cards. So from that point of view, it’s positive. But I’m a player that plays on the edge. It’s something that fuels me and without that edge to my game, sometimes I can potentially go missing. I need to be on the edge to get the best out of myself and unfortunately we are emotional beings, believe it or not, and that does sometimes tip over the edge.” 
 Tough test 
 Cosgrove, who lives with his fiance Laura in the city, loves life here. Particularly because of the weather but also the other opportunities, such as fishing trips, nipping to the beach or playing some of the world’s best golf courses, things that aren’t so readily available in England. 
 Advertisement Advertise with NZME. “You guys in general have got a very good attitude towards life and that’s rubbed off on me,” Cosgrove says. “I’m enjoying myself a hell of a lot more and that does feed into the football.” 
 Sam Cosgrove. Photo / Photosport The only negative? 
 The “weirdly bad drivers” he encounters on a regular basis in his adopted city. 
 “I don’t know whether it’s inconsiderate or maybe a bit spaced out in a world of [their] own but the driving frustrates me. [But] I might upset a few people there.” 
 And is he enjoying sandpapergate, the topic du jour, given Cosgrove played for his county (Cheshire) as a teenage fast bowler? 
 “Probably the only enjoyment I get is the fact that it’s the Aussies.” Cosgrove laughs. “The whole scandal is negative for cricket in general.” 
 Auckland FC face Melbourne Victory today (5pm), with both teams under pressure for a result. A traditional powerhouse, Victory, who have former Black Knights striker Guillermo May in their ranks, have yet to win this season, with three draws and a loss and are ninth on the ladder. However Cosgrove is wary, saying that is a “false position” and more reflective of the toll of their Asian Champions League Two commitments. 
 “It’ll be a tough test,” Cosgrove says. “I thought that they recruited incredibly well in the off-season. Once the league settles down, they’ll be right up there again.” 
 Michael Burgess has been a Sports Journalist for the New Zealand Herald since 2005, covering the Olympics, Fifa World Cups, and America’s Cup campaigns. He is a co-host of the Big League podcast .
